parole.significato: forms feminine singular nouns (roughly equivalent to English -ess or she-)
parole.testo: Inherited from Old Spanish -a, from Latin -a.
Inherited from Old Spanish -abile, from Latin -ābilis.

parole.significato: forms words, derived from nouns, signifying a group (i.e. it forms collective nouns)
parole.testo: Inherited from Latin -āta.

parole.significato: when added to nouns, forms adjectives indicating a characteristic or resemblance; -ate
parole.testo: Inherited from Old Spanish -ado, from Latin -ātus (second declension), from Proto-Italic *-ātos. Doublet of -ato.

parole.significato: when added to nouns, forms nouns indicating a position or domain
parole.testo: Inherited from Old Spanish -ado, from Latin -ātus (fourth declension), formed by rebracketing of action nouns in -tus, -tūs of first conjugation verbs such as mercātus (mercor + -tus), where -ā- is actually part of the stem; from Proto-Italic *-tus, from Proto-Indo-European *-tus (suffix deriving ac
Inherited from Latin -ālis.
From an oblique form *-āmine(m) of Latin -āmen (abstract noun suffix), extended form of -men.
Borrowed from Latin -antia. Compare -anza, which was inherited.

parole.significato: coming from, related to, or like
parole.testo: Inherited from Latin -ānus, which forms adjectives of belonging or origin from a noun.
Inherited from Latin -antia. Compare Catalan -ança, Portuguese -ança, French -ance, Italian -anza.
Inherited from Old Spanish -ar, from Latin -āris.

parole.significato: forms infinitives of first conjugation verbs indicating an action related to the root word
parole.testo: Inherited from Latin -āre (first conjugation infinitive suffix). Cognate with French -er, Italian -are, Romanian -a.
Borrowed from Latin -ārius. Compare the inherited doublet -ero.

parole.significato: -ate (derivative of a salt or ester of an acid whose name ends in -ico)
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from Latin -ātus (second declension), from Proto-Italic *-ātos. These chemistry nouns originated as substantivized perfect passive participles from first conjugation Latin verbs; e.g. the Latin adjective acētātus in the 18th-century Latin phrase plumbum acētātum (“lead acetate”, li
Learned borrowing from Latin -ātus (fourth declension), from Proto-Italic *-tus. Doublet of -ado, which is inherited.

parole.significato: -er, -or forms nouns (usually agent nouns) and adjectives from verbs
parole.testo: Inherited from Latin -tor, from Proto-Italic *-tōr, from Proto-Indo-European *-tōr < *-tor-s.
Inherited from Old Spanish -ecer, from Latin -ēscō, -ēscere.

parole.significato: forms collective nouns, most commonly regarding plants
parole.testo: Inherited from Latin -ētum.

parole.significato: forms diminutives; applies a detestable or vile quality to the root
parole.testo: Inherited from Latin -culus. Doublet of -ículo.
From Latin -entia.

parole.significato: suffix indicating the plural of nouns and adjectives ending in certain consonants (most often -l, -r, -n, -d, -z, -j, -…
parole.testo: From Latin -ēs, the accusative plural ending of most third declension nouns.

parole.significato: attached to adjectives to form abstract nouns of that quality
parole.testo: Inherited from Latin -itia.
Inherited from Latin -ibilis.
Borrowed from Latin -icus, which forms adjectives of belonging or origin from a noun.

parole.significato: diminutive suffix, pejorative in certain regions; forms nouns from nouns; replaces standard Spanish suffix -ito (in Cub…
parole.testo: Related to Ladino -iko, which serves as the equivalent of -ito.

parole.significato: added to feminine nouns to denote a diminutive form
parole.testo: Inherited from Old Spanish -iella, from Latin -ella.

parole.significato: added to masculine nouns to denote a diminutive form
parole.testo: Inherited from Old Spanish -iello, from Latin -ellus, an extension of -lus.

parole.significato: forms diminutives from masculine nouns or adjectives
parole.testo: Inherited from Latin -īnus.

parole.significato: Attaches to an adjective in the feminine singular to form the corresponding adverb; -ly.
parole.testo: Inherited from Old Spanish -mente /-miente /-mientre, from Latin mente.

parole.significato: Used with a stem to form a masculine singular noun.
parole.testo: Inherited from Latin -um, accusative of -us.
Inherited from Latin -tor, from Proto-Italic *-tōr, from Proto-Indo-European *-tōr.
Inherited from Latin -or, from Proto-Italic *-ōs, from Proto-Indo-European *-ōs, from *-os + *-s.
Inherited from Old Spanish -oso, from Latin -ōsus.

parole.significato: forms adjectives and nouns from nouns to indicate that someone or something has a quality in abundance, and sometimes i…
parole.testo: Inherited from Latin -ūtus. Compare Galician -udo, Portuguese -udo, Italian -uto, and French -u.
Inherited from Latin -tiōnem. Doublet of -ción.

parole.significato: forms diminutives of nouns, often already with a diminutive suffix
parole.testo: From Latin -īnus.

parole.significato: forms the absolute superlative of adjectives
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin -issimus, and partly based on the model of Italian -issimo.
Inherited from Latin ad (“to”).

parole.significato: forms words, especially verbs, that denote entering a state, making progress toward a goal, or the like
parole.testo: Inherited from Latin ad-.
Inherited from Old Spanish abierto, from Latin apertus, perfect passive participle of verb aperiō (“to open”). Compare English overt.
Borrowed from Latin acerbus.
Learned borrowing from Latin ācer.

Inherited from Old Spanish agua, from Latin aqua (compare Catalan aigua, French eau, Galician auga, Italian acqua, Occitan aiga, Portuguese água, Romanian apă, Sardinian abba), from Proto-Indo-European *h₂ekʷeh₂. See English ea.
Inherited from Old Spanish ala, from Latin āla. Cognate with Ladino ala.
From Old Spanish alma, inherited from Latin anima. Doublet of ánima, which is borrowed.

Learned borrowing from Latin altus, ultimately of Proto-Indo-European origin. The form alto represents a pronunciation influenced by the most learned layers of the language, and is not the normal phonetic result expected in a naturally inherited word. Cf. the now archaic form oto, which was used mor
Borrowed from Latin anus. False friend to Portuguese ano (“year”).
Inherited from Latin ante.
Borrowed from Latin ante-.
Borrowed from Latin aptus, perfect passive participle of apō.
Inherited from Old Spanish aradro, from Latin arātrum. Compare Catalan arada, Italian aratro Portuguese arado, and Romanian arat.
Inherited from Old Spanish arar, from Latin arō.

Inherited from Latin arcus (whence English archery), from Proto-Indo-European *h₂erkʷo- (“bow, arrow”). In some senses inherited, in others borrowed directly from Latin. Cognate with English arrow, arc, and arch.

Borrowed from Latin argentum, from Proto-Italic *argentom. Borrowed from Latin arguere.
Inherited from Old Spanish arma, from Late Latin arma (“weapon”), from Latin arma (“defensive arms”), from Proto-Indo-European *h₂(e)rmos (“fitting”), from the root *h₂er- (“to join”).
Borrowed from Latin artem (“practical skill”).
Borrowed from Latin aurōra.
Learned borrowing from Latin austrum. Doublet of ostro.
Borrowed from Latin auxilium.
Borrowed from Latin axis. Doublet of eje.
Inherited from Old Spanish anno, from Latin annus (“year”).
Inherited from Latin barba, from earlier *farba, from Proto-Italic *farðā, from Proto-Indo-European *bʰardʰeh₂ (“beard”). Compare English barber.

From Old Spanish bever, inherited from Latin bibere. Cognate with Catalan beure, French boire, Italian bere, Portuguese beber, Romanian bea. The modern spelling with intervocalic ⟨b⟩ replacing medieval ⟨v⟩ is due to Latin influence.
From older beudo, from Old Spanish bebdo, from Late Latin bibitus (“drunk”), perfect passive participle of Latin bibō (“to drink”). Doublet of bebido.
Inherited from Old Spanish bien, from Latin bene (“well”), Old Latin *duenēd, from duenos (“good”), which gave bonus, from Proto-Italic *dwenos.
From Latin bis (“two times”).

parole.significato: fog, mist, especially costal fog or haar
parole.testo: Inherited from Latin brūma.
Inherited from Old Spanish bueno, inherited from Latin bonus (“good”), from Old Latin duenos (later duonus), from Proto-Italic *dwenos. Doublet of bonus, a later borrowing.
From Latin vultus (“face”).

parole.significato: to fit, enter (to be able to be contained (by something; regardless of whether space or volume remains))
parole.testo: Inherited from Old Spanish caber, from Latin capiō, capere (“take, hold, contain”), from Proto-Italic *kapiō, from Proto-Indo-European *kh₂pyéti, from the root *kap- (“to seize, grab”). Inherited from Latin caprum.
Inherited from Old Spanish cagar, from Latin cacāre, from Proto-Italic *kakāō, ultimately from a Proto-Indo-European root *kakka-. Compare English cack.
Inherited from Old Spanish calvo, from Latin calvus.
Inherited from Latin cānus (“white, hoary”), from Proto-Italic *kaznos, from Proto-Indo-European *ḱas-.
Semi-learned borrowing from Latin caput (“head”).
Borrowed from Latin caprīnus. Compare cabra.

parole.significato: flesh, the soft part of a body which covers the bones
parole.testo: Inherited from Old Spanish carne, from Latin carō, carnem (“flesh, meat”). Cognate with Catalan carn, French chair, Italian carne, Portuguese carne, Romanian carne.
Borrowed from Latin cāsus.
Inherited from Old Spanish casto, a learned borrowing from Latin castus.
Borrowed from Latin caterva.
Inherited from Old Spanish ceja, from Latin cilia, plural of cilium (“eyelid”).
Inherited from Latin cēna, from Proto-Italic *kertsnā, from Proto-Indo-European *kért-s-nh₂ (“portion”), from *ker-, *sker-.
Borrowed from Latin centi-, from centum (“hundred”).
Inherited from Latin cernere, cernō, from Proto-Italic *krinō, from Proto-Indo-European *krey-. Doublet of cernir.
Inherited from Old Spanish ciego, from Latin caecus. Compare Italian cieco and Portuguese cego.
Inherited from Old Spanish cielo, from Latin caelum, from Proto-Italic *kailom, from Proto-Indo-European *keh₂i-lom (“whole”), from *keh₂i-.

parole.significato: one hundred (100) (only in compounds followed by lower numerals)
parole.testo: Inherited from Old Spanish, from Latin centum, from Proto-Italic *kəntom, from Proto-Indo-European *ḱm̥tóm.
Inherited from Old Spanish ciervo, from Latin cervus.
Inherited from Old Spanish claro, from Latin clārus. The conservation of Latin /kl-/ is uncommon, with *llaro being the expected outcome. Compare clavo (“nail”) for a similar situation.
Borrowed from Latin classis.
Inherited from Old Spanish color, from Latin colōr.
Inherited from Latin commūnis (inherited as a noun, but as an adjective probably a borrowing or semi-learned term, being first attested relatively late).
Inherited from Latin cum (“with”), from Proto-Italic *kom, from Proto-Indo-European *ḱóm (“next to, at, with, along”). Compare Portuguese com and Italian con.
Inherited from Latin contrā. Old Spanish had cuentra as well, with diphthongization of stressed Latin /ŏ/. As the word was generally atonic, the unstressed variant contra prevailed over time.

parole.significato: to agree, agree on, agree upon
parole.testo: Inherited from Latin convenīre.
Borrowed from Latin cornū. Doublet of cuerno.
Inherited from Old Spanish correr, from Latin currere.
Inherited from Latin curvus.

Inherited from Old Spanish cresçer, from Latin crēscĕre, from Proto-Italic *krēskō, from Proto-Indo-European *ḱreh₁- (“to grow, become bigger”). Compare French croître, Italian crescere and English crescent.
Borrowed from Latin credō (“to believe”). Doublet of creo.
Learned borrowing from Latin crīmen (“verdict; crime”).
Inherited from Old Spanish crudo, from Latin crūdus. Cognate with English crude, French cru, and Italian crudo.
Inherited from Latin crucem.
Borrowed from Latin quadri-.

parole.significato: like, as, in the manner of
parole.testo: Inherited from Latin quālis.

parole.significato: whatever quantity, as much, however much
parole.testo: Inherited from Latin quantus, from Proto-Italic *kʷijentos, from Proto-Indo-European *kʷíh₂onts (“how much, how many”), from *kʷíh₂, neuter of *kʷís. Cognate with French quant, Italian quanto, Portuguese quanto, Romanian cât, Ashkun ćīt, Waigali kiti, Sanskrit कियत् (kíyat), Avestan 𐬗𐬎𐬎𐬀𐬧𐬙 (cuuaṇt).

Inherited from Old Spanish quatro, from Latin quattŭor (“four”), from Proto-Italic *kʷettwōr, from Proto-Indo-European *kʷetwóres. Cognates include Ancient Greek τέσσαρες (téssares), French quatre, Old English feower (English four).
Inherited from Latin corium (“skin; hide, leather”). Sense 4 probably as a euphemism for cuerpo (“body”).

parole.significato: body (the physical structure of a human or animal)
parole.testo: Inherited from Old Spanish cuerpo, from Latin corpus. Doublet of corpus (a borrowing).

parole.significato: summit, peak, top, hilltop (topmost point or surface, especially of a mountain)
parole.testo: Inherited from Latin culminem, from Proto-Italic *kolamen, from Proto-Indo-European *kelH-. The sense of “gathering” is a calque of English summit. Doublet of culmen.
Inherited from Old Spanish cuna, from Latin cūna, cūnae, from Proto-Italic *koinā, from Proto-Indo-European *ḱoyneh₂, derived from the root *ḱey- (“to be lying down; to settle”).
Learned borrowing from Latin curvus (“bent”). Doublet of corvo, which was inherited.
Inherited from Old Spanish qual, from Latin quālis (“which”).

From earlier quánto, from Latin quantus, from Proto-Italic *kʷijentos, from Proto-Indo-European *kʷíh₂onts (“how much, how many”), from *kʷíh₂, neuter of *kʷís. Cognate with French quant, Italian quanto, Portuguese quanto, Romanian cât, Ashkun ćī́t, Waigali kiti, Sanskrit कियत् (kíyat), Avestan 𐬗𐬎𐬎𐬀
Borrowed from Latin cancer. Compare cangrejo, inherited from a Vulgar Latin diminutive form.
Inherited from Old Spanish dar (“to give”), from Latin dare.

parole.significato: of; 's; used after the thing owned and before the owner
parole.testo: Inherited from Old Spanish de, from Latin dē, from Proto-Italic *dē, from Proto-Indo-European *déh₁, from *de + *-h₁. Cognate with Ladino de.
Inherited from Latin dē-.
From Latin dea.

parole.significato: to say, to tell, to name, to mention
parole.testo: Inherited from Old Spanish dezir, from Latin dīcere, from Proto-Italic *deikō, from Proto-Indo-European *déyḱeti (“to show, point out”).
Inherited from Old Spanish des-, from Latin dis-, from Proto-Indo-European *dwís. Doublet of dis-, which was borrowed.
From Latin dis- or Latin dī-.
Inherited from Old Spanish diente (“tooth”), from Latin dēns, dentem.

Inherited from Old Spanish diez (“ten”), from Latin decem, from Proto-Indo-European *déḱm̥. Cognates include French dix and Portuguese dez; more distantly Ancient Greek δέκα (déka), English ten, and German zehn.
Borrowed from Latin dignus. Compare the older form dino, which it replaced.

Inherited from Old Spanish dios, from Latin deus (“god, deity”), from Old Latin deivos (“god, deity”), from Proto-Italic *deiwos (“god, deity”), from Proto-Indo-European *deywós (“god, deity”), from *dyew- (“sky, heaven”). The form in -os continues the Latin nominative, not the expected accusative a
Borrowed from Latin dīvīnus.

parole.significato: to hurt (to cause physical or emotional pain)
parole.testo: Inherited from Old Spanish doler, inherited from Latin dolēre, doleō, from Proto-Italic *doleō (“hurt, cause pain”), from Proto-Indo-European *dolh₁éyeti (“divide”), from *delh₁- (“cut”). Compare English condolence.
Inherited from Old Spanish domar, from Latin domāre.
Inherited from Latin dōnāre.
Inherited from Old Spanish dormir, from Latin dormīre, from Proto-Italic *dormiō, from Proto-Indo-European *dr̥m-yé-ti, from *drem- (“to sleep”) + *-yéti.

Inherited from Old Spanish dos, from Latin duōs, from Proto-Italic *duō, from Proto-Indo-European *dwóh₁. Cognates include Ancient Greek δύο (dúo), Old English twa (English two), Persian دو.  PIE word  *dwóh₁
Inherited from Latin dūcere.

Inherited from Old Spanish duro, from Latin dūrus, from Proto-Italic *dūros, from Proto-Indo-European *duh₂-ró-s (“long”), from *dweh₂- (“far, long”). Cognate with Ancient Greek δηρός (dērós, “long”), Sanskrit दूर (dūrá, “distant, far, long”). Compare English dour & English durable.
Borrowed from Latin domine.
Inherited from Latin et.
Borrowed from Latin ēbrius.
Inherited from Old Spanish edat, from Latin aetās. Cognate with English age, eternity, and eon.
Borrowed from Latin ego (“I”). Doublet of yo.
Inherited from Old Spanish en, from Latin in, from Old Latin en, from Proto-Italic *en, from Proto-Indo-European *h₁én.
Inherited from Old Spanish en-, from Latin in-, prefixation of Latin in (“in, into”); see en.
Inherited from Latin inter-. Doublet of inter-.
Inherited from Old Spanish es-, from Latin ex- (“out of”). Doublet of ex-, which is borrowed.

parole.testo: Inherited from Latin scamnum, from Proto-Italic *skaβnom, from Proto-Indo-European *skabʰ-no-m, from *skabʰ- (“to hold up”). Cognate with Galician escano, Portuguese escano, Italian scanno, and more distantly Sanskrit स्कम्भ (skambhá).
Borrowed from Latin scindere.
Inherited from Latin scriptum.
Inherited from Old Spanish espina, from Latin spīna.
Borrowed from Latin spina.
Borrowed from Latin statuō.

parole.significato: star; stellar (of or relating to stars)

Learned borrowing from Latin stilus.
Inherited from Old Spanish estrecho, from Latin strictus. Doublet of estricto, a learned borrowing from Latin.

Inherited from Old Spanish estrella, from Latin stēlla, probably through an unattested regional Latin *strēlla. Cognate with Asturian estrella, Catalan estrella, Galician estrela, and Portuguese estrela.
Inherited from Latin stellāris.

From Latin stipula (“string, straw”).
Borrowed from Latin et.
Learned borrowing from Latin aevum.
From Latin ex.
Borrowed from Latin factum. Compare the inherited doublet hecho.

Derived from Latin foedus.
Borrowed from Latin fēriae.
Learned borrowing from Latin ferōx (“wild, untamed”).
Learned borrowing from Latin fētus.

parole.significato: edge, cutting edge (of the blade of an instrument)

Both were inherited, and it is not entirely clear why the two diverged in pronunciation, with filo coming to mean 'edge' and hilo maintaining the Latin sense of 'string, thread'. Perhaps the /f~h/ variation was exploited t
Borrowed from Latin flāgrō.
Borrowed from Latin flamma.

Inherited from Old Spanish flor, from Latin flōs (accusative flōrem). Inherited from Old Spanish, from Latin fundus  PIE word  *bʰudʰmḗn The preservation of the initial older 'f' in this word may be to distinguish it from the doublet hondo, which became an adjective and continued its phonetic evolution as expected. Also the doublet of fundo, a later borrowing.
Borrowed from Latin forum. Doublet of fuero.
Inherited from Old Spanish fresno, freisno, frexno, frexeno, Latin fraxinus (“ash tree”), from *bʰr̥Hǵ-s-inos, adjective of Proto-Indo-European *bʰerHǵos (“birch”).
Borrowed from Latin fruī.
Inherited from Old Spanish fuero, from Latin forum, from Proto-Italic *forom, from *fworom, from *θworom, from Proto-Indo-European *dʰwór-o-, from *dʰwer- + *-os. Doublet of foro.
Borrowed from Latin fuga.
Learned borrowing from Latin fulgēre.
Inherited from Old Spanish fundir, a learned borrowing from Latin fundō. Doublet of hundir (“to sink”). Cognate with English found (“to melt”) and fuse.
Borrowed from Latin fundus. Doublet of fondo.
Borrowed from Latin germen (“germ, seed”).
Borrowed from Latin gluten (“glue”).
Inherited from Old Spanish grave, from Latin gravis. Cf. also the attested Old Spanish form grieve, from Early Medieval Latin grevis, which was more common in other Romance-speaking areas.

Borrowed from Latin gustus (“taste”), from Proto-Italic *gustus, from Proto-Indo-European *ǵéwstus. Replaced the inherited Old Spanish form gosto. The learned word has a more abstract meaning overall.

parole.significato: to have; forms the perfect aspect
parole.testo: Latinised respelling of Old Spanish aver, from Latin habēre, habeō (“have, hold”), probably from Proto-Italic *habēō or *haβēō, ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *gʰeh₁bʰ- (“to grab, take”). Cognate with French avoir, Italian avere, Occitan aver, Portuguese haver, Romanian avea, avere, and Sardini

Inherited from Old Spanish fazer, from Latin facere. The first-person indicative (hago) and present subjunctive forms (haga, hagas, etc.) may have been influenced by Latin agō (compare English gesture), but more likely come from a voicing of intervocalic Latin /k/ after having dropped /i/ (e.g. Lati
Inherited from Latin fātum. Doublet of fado.
Inherited from Old Spanish faya, from Latin [materia] fāgea, from fāgus, from Proto-Italic *fāgos, from Proto-Indo-European *bʰeh₂ǵos. Compare Galician and Portuguese faia.

Inherited from Old Spanish femna, fembra, from Latin fēmina (“female”), from Proto-Italic *fēmanā, from Proto-Indo-European *dʰeh₁-m̥h₁n-eh₂ (“(f.) one who is sucked; one who suckles”), derivation of the verbal root *dʰeh₁(y)- (“to suck, suckle”). Doublet of fémina, which is a direct borrowing.
Inherited from Old Spanish fender, from Latin findere, findō, from Proto-Italic *findō, from Proto-Indo-European *bʰeyd- (“to split”).

parole.significato: to wound, injure (cause physical injury and pain)
parole.testo: Inherited from Old Spanish ferir, from Latin feriō, -īre (“to hit”). Related to English interfere.
Inherited from Old Spanish ermana, from Latin germāna.
Inherited from Old Spanish ermano, from Vulgar Latin *germānus (“brother”), from Latin germānus (“of a brother or sister”). Compare English germane. Displaced Old Spanish fradre, from fratēr.
Inherited from Old Spanish *fennir, from Latin fingere. See also the borrowed doublet fingir.
Inherited from Old Spanish fijo, from Latin fīlius.

Inherited from Old Spanish omne, from Latin hominem, homō, from Old Latin hemō, from Proto-Indo-European *ǵʰmṓ (“earthling”). Inherited from Old Spanish formiga, from Latin formīca.
Inherited from Old Spanish forno, from Latin furnus.
Borrowed from Latin horrendus.

Inherited from Old Spanish huesso, from Latin ossum, popular variant of os, ossis, from Proto-Italic *ōs, ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *h₃ésth₁ (“bone”), *h₂óst. Inherited from Latin hostem (“enemy, stranger”), from Proto-Italic *hostim, from Proto-Indo-European *gʰóstim (“guest, stranger”). Compare Catalan host (“army”), Italian oste (“army, host”), Romanian oaste (“army, host”).
Inherited from Old Spanish fumo, from Latin fūmus. Doublet of fumo. Compare Ladino umo.
Inherited from Old Spanish fundir. Doublet of fundir (“to cast, melt”), from Latin fundere. Compare English found (“to cast metal”), founder (“to sink”).

Inherited from Old Spanish huésped, from Latin hospitem, from Proto-Italic *hostipotis, an old compound of hostis and the root of potis, possibly corresponding to a Proto-Indo-European root *gʰóstipotis, a compound of *gʰóstis and *pótis. Doublet of host. See also hueste.
Borrowed from Latin in- (“un-, not”).
Borrowed from Latin in- (“inward”).
Inherited from Old Spanish infierno, from Latin īnfernum.
Learned borrowing from Latin inter-. Doublet of entre-.
Inherited from Old Spanish joven, a semi-learned borrowing from Latin iuvenis.
Learned borrowing from Latin iūbilāre. Cognate with English jubilate.
Inherited from Latin iūnctus (“joined, united”).
Inherited from Old Spanish justo, inherited from Latin iūstus, jūstus, from Proto-Italic *jowestos, from Proto-Indo-European *h₂yew-.
From Old Spanish ela, from Latin illa(m), feminine singular of ille.
Inherited from Old Spanish lago, from Latin lacus.
Inherited from Old Spanish lana, from Latin lāna. Cognate with Catalan llana, Galician la, French laine, Occitan lana, Portuguese lã, Romanian lână, Italian lana.
From Old Spanish lavar, from Latin lavāre (“to wash”).
Inherited from Old Spanish leer, from Latin legēre (“to collect, gather; to read”). Cognate with English legend, legible, lesson.
Inherited from Old Spanish lengua, from Latin lingua. Cognate with English tongue and language.

Borrowed from Latin lentus. Compare the inherited Old Spanish form liento (“humid, wet”), which has a meaning also found in some senses of Galician and Portuguese lento, Asturian llentu; cf. also Valencian Catalan llenta.
Inherited from Old Spanish ley, from Latin lēgem (whence English legal and legitimate), from Proto-Italic *lēg-, from Proto-Indo-European *leǵ-s, from *leǵ- (“to gather”).
Probably borrowed from Latin līber, from Old Latin loeber, from Proto-Italic *louðeros, from Proto-Indo-European *h₁lewdʰ-er-os, from *h₁lewdʰ- (“people”).
Inherited from Old Spanish libro, a learned borrowing from Latin liber (“book”). Cognate with Asturian llibru, Catalan llibre, French livre, Galician libro, Italian libro, and Portuguese livro.

Inherited from Old Spanish llaga, from Latin plāga (“hit, strike”). Cognate with Asturian llaga, Catalan plaga, French plaie, Galician and Portuguese chaga, Italian piaga, Romanian plagă, and more distantly with Ancient Greek πληγή (plēgḗ, “wound”). Doublet of plaga (“plague”).
Inherited from Old Spanish llama, from Latin flamma.
Inherited from Latin plānus. Compare the borrowed doublets plano and piano. Cognate with Galician chan, Italian piano, and Portuguese chão.
Inherited from Latin clāvis (“key”), from Proto-Italic *klāwis, of ultimately Proto-Indo-European origin. Doublet of clave. Cognate with English clef.

Inherited from Old Spanish lleno, lenno, inherited from Latin plēnus, whence also Spanish pleno, which is a borrowed doublet. The Latin word derives from Proto-Italic *plēnos, from Proto-Indo-European *pl̥h₁nós (“full”).

parole.significato: an enclosed arable land next to a house
parole.testo: Inherited from Latin clausa (“enclosed”). Compare with Galician and Portuguese chousa.
Learned borrowing from Latin locus. Doublet of luego.

Inherited from Old Spanish luego (“then”), from Latin locō (“in the place of, instead of, for”), ablative of locus, from Old Latin stlocus, from Proto-Indo-European *stel- (“to put, place, locate”). Doublet of locus. Cognate with English lieu and locus.
Inherited from Old Spanish luengo, from Latin longus. Cognate with English long.

From Old Spanish lumbre, lumne, from Latin lūmen (“light source”). First attested in the Cantar de mio Cid. The shift /mn/ > /mbɾ/ is regular and expected: compare hambre and hombre. Cognate with Aragonese llumbre, lumbre, Asturian llume, Catalan llum, Galician and Portuguese lume, Italian lume, and
Learned borrowing from Latin lūx. Doublet of the inherited luz.
Inherited from Old Spanish luz, from Latin lūx.
Borrowed from Latin lapidem, from Proto-Italic *lapets, possibly from Proto-Indo-European *lep-. Doublet of lápiz and probably laude.

Possibly from Latin lūbricus (“slippery, slimy”). Perhaps influenced by lūgubris (“gloomy, mournful”). Doublet of lúbrico. Cognate with Portuguese lôbrego and Asturian llóbregu. An alternative theory derives the term directly from lūgubris, with metathesis; in which case the doublet would be lúgubre
Learned borrowing from Latin lūbricus. Compare lóbrego, probably a doublet.
Inherited from Latin mātrem (“mother, matron”), from Proto-Italic *mātēr, from Proto-Indo-European *méh₂tēr. Compare English matron.
Inherited from Latin magistrum. Doublet of magíster, borrowed from Latin, and máster, borrowed from English.
Borrowed from Latin magnus (“big, large”), from Proto-Italic *magnos, from Proto-Indo-European *m̥ǵh₂nós, from *méǵh₂s (“great”). Doublet of maño.
Inherited from Latin macrum, from Proto-Indo-European *mh₂ḱrós. Cognate with English meager /meagre.
Inherited from Latin male.
Inherited from Old Spanish malo, from Latin malus. Cognate with Ladino malo, Italian malo, Galician mao, Portuguese mau.

Inherited from Old Spanish mano, from Latin manus, from Proto-Italic *manus, perhaps from Proto-Indo-European *méh₂-r̥ ~ *mh₂-én-, derived from Proto-Indo-European *(s)meh₂- (“to beckon”), or perhaps from Proto-Indo-European *mon-u- (see the Proto-Italic entry). Cognate with Galician man and Portugu
Inherited from Old Spanish mar (“sea”), from Latin mare (“sea”), from Proto-Italic *mari, from Proto-Indo-European *móri. osp + mar. Compare French mer, Italian mare, Portuguese mar, Romanian mare.
Inherited from Latin maior.
Uncertain if inherited or semi-borrowed from Latin magnus (“big, large”), from Proto-Italic *magnos, from Proto-Indo-European *m̥ǵh₂nós, from *méǵh₂s (“great”). Doublet of magno.
Inherited from Latin miscēre. Compare Portuguese mexer.

parole.significato: half (of or related to one of two equal divisions of a whole)
parole.testo: Borrowed directly from Latin medius (“half”) rather than inherited through an Old Spanish form, possibly because the likely forms *meo and *meyo would have closely resembled mear (“to piss”), ultimately from Proto-Italic *meðjos, from Proto-Indo-European *médʰyos (“between”). Compare Portuguese meio
Inherited from Latin mēnsis (“month”). Compare Catalan mes, Italian mese, Portuguese mês, Romansh mais.

Inherited from Old Spanish meter, from Latin mittere (“to send”). The semantic shift from "send" to "put" probably occurred in Vulgar Latin. Cognate with English mess and also mission, message. Compare also French mettre, Friulian meti, Portuguese meter, and Italian mettere.

parole.significato: member (one who belongs to a group)
parole.testo: Inherited from Latin membrum, from Proto-Italic *memzrom, from Proto-Indo-European *mḗms, *mēms-rom (“flesh”). Cognate with Asturian miembru, Galician membro.
Inherited from Latin mentem.

parole.significato: shit (solid excretory product evacuated from the bowels; feces.)
parole.testo: Inherited from Old Spanish mierda, from Latin merda, from Proto-Italic *(s)merdā, from Proto-Indo-European *smerd-h₂- (“stench”). Cognate with Italian merda, Portuguese merda, Catalan merda, Galician merda, French merde and the obsolete English merd.
Inherited from Latin milium, from Proto-Italic *meljom, from Proto-Indo-European *melh₂- (“to grind, crush”). Doublet of millo.
Inherited from Old Spanish mil, mill, from Latin mīlle.
Borrowed from Latin ministrum.
Inherited from Old Spanish moco, from Latin muccus, variant of mūcus.
Inherited from Old Spanish moler, from Latin molō.
Borrowed from Latin mōmentum.
Inherited from Latin mōns (accusative montem).
Inherited from Old Spanish morder, from Latin mordēre.

parole.significato: to move (to cause to change place or posture)
parole.testo: Inherited from Old Spanish mover, from Latin movēre. Cognate with English move.

Inherited from Old Spanish mucho, muito, from Latin multus (“much, many”), from the Proto-Indo-European *ml̥tos (“crumbled, crumpled”, past passive participle). Compare the Portuguese muito (“much, many, a lot”). Unrelated to English much, which is related to archaic maño (“big”) (the second element
Inherited from Old Spanish muela (“millstone”), from Latin mola.

parole.significato: fine (a fee levied as punishment for breaking the law)
parole.testo: From Latin multa.
Inherited from Old Spanish muro, from Latin mūrus. Cognate with German Mauer (“wall”) and obsolete English mure. Compare English mural.

parole.significato: to arrange or dispose of a matter of business
parole.testo: Inherited from Latin monēre.

parole.significato: macula (spot near the center of the retina)
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin macula. Doublet of mancha.
Learned borrowing from Latin maximus.
Learned borrowing from Latin meritum (“merit”).
Borrowed from Latin miserum.
Borrowed from Latin nātiōnem.
Borrowed from Latin nātus.

parole.significato: Used when negating two or more elements, and not, not A or B, not A nor B, neither A nor B
parole.testo: From Old Spanish nin, from Latin nec, apocopated form of neque, from Proto-Indo-European *nekʷe (“and not, neither, nor”), from *né (“not”) + *-kʷe (“and”). Compare Asturian and Galician nin, Catalan and French ni, Portuguese nem, Italian né, Dalmatian ne. Indo-European cognates include Gothic 𐌽𐌹𐌷 (
Inherited from Old Spanish nido, from Latin nīdus.

parole.significato: night (the period between sunset and sunrise)
parole.testo: Inherited from Old Spanish noche, from Latin nox, from Proto-Italic *nok⁽ʷ⁾ts, from Proto-Indo-European *nókʷts.
Inherited from Old Spanish nombre, nomne, from Latin nōmen.
From Latin nonus.
Borrowed from Latin nota.
Borrowed from Latin novāre.
Inherited from Latin novembrem.
Inherited from Old Spanish nuestro, Latin nostrum, from Proto-Italic *nosteros.
Inherited from Old Spanish nuevo, from Latin novus.
Borrowed from Latin nullus (“none”).
Borrowed from Latin nū̆cleus (“kernel, core”).
Borrowed from Latin numerus, ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *nem- (“to assign, allot; take”).

Inherited from Old Spanish ocho, from an earlier *oito, from Latin octō, from Proto-Indo-European *oḱtṓw. Cognates include Ancient Greek ὀκτώ (oktṓ), Portuguese oito, Old English eahta (English eight).
Inherited from Old Spanish oler, from Latin oleō. Cognate with English olfactor and odor.

parole.significato: pot, pan; kettle (vessel used for cooking food)
parole.testo: Inherited from Old Spanish olla, from Latin ōlla, from Proto-Italic *aukslā, from Proto-Indo-European *Hukʷsleh₂, Proto-Indo-European *Hukʷ- (“cooking pot”).
Semi-learned borrowing from Latin ōrdinem m. Cognate with English order.
Borrowed from Latin orientem.

Inherited from Old Spanish oro, from Latin aurum (compare Catalan or, Dalmatian jaur, French or, Galician ouro, Italian oro, Occitan aur, Portuguese ouro, Romanian aur), from Proto-Italic *auzom, from Proto-Indo-European *h₂é-h₂us-o- (“glow”). Cognate with English aurum.
Inherited from Old Spanish osso, from Vulgar Latin *ussus, from Latin ursus. Compare Asturian osu, Aragonese onso, Catalan ós, Galician oso, Portuguese urso.

Inherited from Old Spanish oueja, from Latin ovicula (“little sheep”), diminutive of ovis (“sheep”), from Proto-Italic *owis, from Proto-Indo-European *h₂ówis. Compare Portuguese ovelha, Russian овца (ovca)
Learned borrowing from Latin ōvum. Doublet of huevo.
Inherited from Old Spanish pascer, from Latin pāscere.
Inherited from Old Spanish padre (“father”), from Latin patrem, pater, from Proto-Italic *patēr, from Proto-Indo-European *ph₂tḗr.

Inherited from Latin pālus (“stake”), from Proto-Italic *pākslos, from Proto-Indo-European *peh₂ǵ-slos, from *peh₂ǵ-. Cognate with English pole and pale (“fence post”). Compare the vulgar reference to the penis with Portuguese pau.

parole.significato: part; section; portion; share; piece; bit; cut; proportion
parole.testo: Inherited from Old Spanish parte (“part”), from Latin partem, from Proto-Italic *partim.
From Old Spanish passo, from Latin passus, -um (“step, pace”). Cognate with Catalan pas, English pace and pass, French pas, Galician paso, Portuguese passo, and Romanian pas.
Borrowed from Latin patrōnus. Doublet of padrón.
Inherited from Old Spanish paz, from Latin pācem, from Proto-Indo-European *peh₂ǵ-.

Inherited from Old Spanish pecar, a learned borrowing from Latin peccāre. If directly inherited, short Latin /e/ would have diphthongized into Spanish /je/ when stressed, e.g. yielding *pieco instead of peco (“I sin”).

Inherited from Latin pectus, from Proto-Italic *pektos, from Proto-Indo-European *peg- (“breast”). Compare Catalan pit, Italian petto, Portuguese peito, Romanian piept. See also peto, a doublet borrowed from Italian.
Borrowed from Latin pecūlium (“property, savings”). Compare Aragonese pegullo, which was inherited.
Inherited from Latin pēdere, pēdō, from Proto-Italic *pezdō from Proto-Indo-European *pesd-.
Inherited from Old Spanish peyne, from Latin pecten (through the accusative pectinem).

Inherited from Old Spanish pender, from Latin pendēre, pendeō, from Proto-Italic *pendēō, from Proto-Indo-European *(s)pend- (“to pull; to spin”). That it was inherited is shown by medieval diphthongized conjugations such as piende or the past participle pendudo. Subsequently it became an increasing
Learned borrowing from Latin pēnis.

parole.significato: to weigh (to determine the weight of an object)
parole.testo: Inherited from Old Spanish pesar, from Latin pēnsāre, whence also the doublet pensar 'think'. Cognate with English poise, French peser, Italian pesare, Portuguese pesar, and Romanian păsa.

Inherited from Old Spanish pie, from Latin pedem, from Proto-Italic *pets, from Proto-Indo-European *pṓds, from *ped- + *-s. Cognate with Asturian pie, Galician and Portuguese pé, Catalan peu, and further English foot. As an English unit, a semantic loan from English foot.
Inherited from Old Spanish piel, pielle, from Latin pellis, pellem.
Inherited from Latin pīnus, ultimately from a derivative of Proto-Indo-European *poi- (“sap, juice”). Cognate with English pine.
Learned borrowing from Latin plāga. Doublet of llaga.
Inherited from Old Spanish plano, a learned borrowing from Latin plānus. Compare llano, a doublet inherited from the same source.

parole.significato: plant (an organism of the kingdom Plantae, and now specifically, a living organism of the Embryophyta (land plants) or…
parole.testo: Inherited from Old Spanish planta (“plant”), borrowed from Latin planta, from Proto-Italic *plāntā, from Proto-Indo-European *pléh₂-n̥t-eh₂, from *pleh₂- (“flat”). Compare the now obsolete inherited form llanta.
Borrowed from Latin plūs (“more”).
Inherited from Old Spanish pobre, from Latin pauper, -erem. Cognate with English pauper.
Inherited from Old Spanish poco, from Latin paucus. Cognate with Catalan poc, French peu, Italian poco, and Portuguese pouco, as well as English few.

parole.significato: to put, to place (cause to assume a specified position)
parole.testo: Inherited from Latin pōnere (whence English post and position), from Proto-Italic *pozinō. Compare Portuguese pôr and Romanian pune.
From Latin post (“after, behind”). Cognate with English post-
Borrowed from Latin prae- (“before”), from the Latin preposition prae.
Inherited from Old Spanish prea, from Latin praeda. Doublet of presa.
Borrowed from Late Latin praebenda, from Latin praebendus.
Inherited from Old Spanish prender, from Latin prēndere, from earlier prehendere.
Borrowed from Latin prīmus (“first”), from earlier prīsmos < *prīsemos < Proto-Italic *priisemos (“foremost”, superlative of pri, "before, in front").
Borrowed from Latin prīmōris (“foremost”).
Borrowed from Latin probus.
Inherited from Old Spanish pueblo, from Latin populus (“people, nation”), from Proto-Italic *poplos (“army”).

Inherited from Old Spanish puerco, from Latin porcus, from Proto-Italic *porkos, from Proto-Indo-European *pórḱos (“young swine, young pig”). The "police officer" slang sense is apparently a semantic loan from English pig.

parole.significato: door (portal of entry into a building)
parole.testo: Inherited from Old Spanish puerta, from Latin porta.
Inherited from Old Spanish punto, from Latin pūnctum (“point”), from pungō (“to prick, puncture”). Cognate with Asturian puntu, Catalan punt Galician punto, Portuguese ponto.

parole.significato: fist (hand with the fingers clenched or curled inward)
parole.testo: Inherited from Old Spanish punno, from Latin pugnus.
Learned borrowing from Latin pūblicus.
Inherited from Latin quid (“what”), but usurping all the roles of Latin quod. Cognate with English who.
Inherited from Latin quī.
Inherited from Latin quĕm, accusative of quī, from Old Latin quei, from Proto-Italic *kʷoi, from Proto-Indo-European *kʷís, *kʷos.
Inherited from Latin quem.
Inherited from Latin quid.
Inherited from Old Spanish rabo, from Latin rāpum (“turnip”). Cognate with English rape as in rapeseed the plant.
Inherited from Old Spanish ramo, from Latin rāmus, from Proto-Italic *wrād-mo-, from Proto-Indo-European *wréh₂dmos, from *wréh₂ds (“root”).

From Latin rāta (“considered, established, certain”, adjective) through ellipsis of phrases such as rāta parte (“established part”), rāta ratiōne (“established ration”) etc., feminine ablative singular of ratus, perfect active participle of rērī (“to think, judge, consider”). Cognate with English ra
Inherited from Latin rādīcem, from Proto-Italic *wrādīks, from Proto-Indo-European *wréh₂ds. Cognate with English radish.
From Latin re-. The use with adjectives is typical of Ibero-Romance. Compare Italian stra- (from Latin extra-), French très (from Latin trans-; now spelt separate, but formerly also a prefix).

parole.significato: to rule, govern, be in charge of, reign
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from Latin regere.

parole.significato: head of quadrupedal livestock or game (e.g. cattle, sheep, deer)
parole.testo: Inherited from Old Spanish res, from the nominative of Latin rēs (“thing, property”). Cognate with Aragonese, Asturian, Catalan, and Galician res and Portuguese rês. A derivation from Arabic رَأْس (raʔs, “head”, also of cattle) is almost unanimously described in dictionaries and represents a perfect
Borrowed from Latin retrō.
A learned formation stemming from Latin revīsus (may also be seen as a compound of re- + visar). Compare French réviser; cf. also Latin reviso, revisere.
Inherited from Latin rīpa.
From Old Spanish roxo, inherited from Latin russus or russeus. Compare Portuguese roxo.
Borrowed from Latin rubus, from Proto-Italic *wruðos, from Proto-Indo-European *wr̥dʰo- (“sweetbriar”).

parole.significato: wheel (a circular device capable of rotating on its axis, facilitating movement or transportation or performing labour…
parole.testo: Inherited from Old Spanish rueda, from Latin rota. Cognate with Catalan, Galician, and Portuguese roda (“wheel”), French roue (“wheel”), Italian ruota (“wheel”), Mirandese ruodra (“wheel”), and Romanian roată (“wheel”). Related to rodar and rotar.
Inherited from Latin rūga.
Borrowed from Latin sacrum.
Inherited from Latin sacrātus.

Inherited from Old Spanish sal, from Latin salem (compare Catalan sal f, French sel m, Italian sale m, Portuguese sal m, Romanian sare f; also English salt). It is not known how the noun became feminine.

parole.significato: to go out, to leave, to depart, to head out
parole.testo: Inherited from Old Spanish salir, from Latin salīre. Compare Portuguese sair and Romanian sări. Cognate with English sally. Displaced in meaning by the doublet saltar.
Borrowed from Latin salūbrem.

Inherited from Old Spanish sangne, from Latin sanguis, sanguinem. The shift from /n/ to /ɾ/ in was likely due to dissimilation of two subsequent nasal consonants. The reason for the change in gender is unclear Cognate with Asturian sangre, Catalan sang, Galician sangue, French sang, Italian sangue,
Inherited from Old Spanish santo, sancto, from Latin sānctus.

parole.significato: silk (fine fiber excreted by the silkworm or other arthropod)
parole.testo: Inherited from Old Spanish seda, from Latin sēta, monophthongized variant of saeta, from Proto-Italic *saitā, from Proto-Indo-European *séh₂ito-, *sh₂éyto-, from *sh₂ey-, *seh₂i- (“to bind”).
Inherited from Old Spanish segar, from Latin secāre. Unrelated to secar (“to dry”), which is from Latin siccāre.
Inherited from Latin secundus with, per Coromines, a 'semi-learned' treatment of the stressed vowel (*segondo would have been expected otherwise). Doublet of según. Related to seguir (“follow”).
Inherited from Latin sex, from Proto-Indo-European *swéḱs. Cognates include Ancient Greek ἕξ (héx), French six, Old English six (English six).
Borrowed from Latin sēmen.
Semi-learned modification of earlier setiembre, based on the Latin septembrem.

parole.significato: snake, serpent (legless reptile of the sub-order Serpentes)
parole.testo: Inherited from Old Spanish serpiente, from Latin serpentem. Doublet of sierpe. Cognate with English serpent.

parole.significato: to serve (to be a servant or worker; to render service)
parole.testo: Inherited from Latin servīre.
From Latin sextum. By surface analysis, sexto + -eto.
Inherited from Latin si (“if”).
Inherited from Latin septem, from Proto-Indo-European *septḿ̥. Cognates include Ancient Greek ἑπτά (heptá), Italian sette, French sept, Portuguese sete, Old English seofon (English seven).
Inherited from Old Spanish sieglo, siglo, siclo, a semi-learned term derived from Latin saeculum (the expected popularly inherited result would be *sejo or *siejo).

Inherited from Old Spanish syguiente, from the old present participle of seguir. Corresponds to Latin sequentem (“following”), the present active participle of sequor (“to follow”), from Proto-Italic *sekʷōr, from Proto-Indo-European *sekʷ- (“to follow”). Compare English sequential.

Inherited from Old Spanish siella (“chair, saddle”), from Latin sella. Cognate with Asturian and Leonese siella (“chair”), Catalan sella (“saddle”), French selle (“saddle”), Galician and Portuguese sela (“saddle”), Italian sella (“saddle”), and Romanian șa (“saddle”); as well as distantly English sa
Learned borrowing from Latin sincērus.
Inherited from Latin sub, from Proto-Italic *supo, from Proto-Indo-European *upo.
Inherited from Latin sub-. Doublet of sub-, which was borrowed.
Inherited from Latin super-. Doublet of super-.
Borrowed from Latin socius (“partaking, associated; partner, associate”).
Borrowed from Latin suāvis (“sweet, pleasant”).
Borrowed from Latin sub-. Doublet of so-, which was inherited.
Inherited from Old Spanish suerte, from Latin sortem, from Proto-Italic *sortis, from Proto-Indo-European *ser- (“to bind”). Compare Portuguese sorte, Galician sorte.

Inherited from Old Spanish suenno, from Latin somnus (“sleep”), from Proto-Italic *swepnos, from Proto-Indo-European *swépnos. Compare Portuguese sono, Italian sonno (“sleep”) and Sicilian sonnu (“sleep”).
Borrowed from Latin summa. Doublet of soma (“coarse flour”), which is inherited.
Borrowed from Latin summus. Compare the inherited Old Spanish somo, cf. also Spanish somero.
Learned borrowing from Latin super-. Doublet of sobre-.
Borrowed from Latin similis.
Borrowed from Latin solidus (“solid”).
Borrowed from Latin solidus (“gold coin”). Doublet of the inherited sueldo.
Borrowed from Latin tangentem.

parole.significato: daddy; dad, a term used by children for their father
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin tata. Compare taita.
Inherited from Latin tangere, tangō, from Proto-Italic *tangō, nasal infix present from Proto-Indo-European *teh₂g-. Doublet of tangir, a learned borrowing.
Inherited from Latin tēctum. Compare Portuguese teto, Galician teito, French toit and Italian tetto.

Inherited from Old Spanish texer, from Latin texere (“to weave, intertwine”). Doublet of texto and textil. Cognate with Asturian texer, Catalan teixir, and Galician and Portuguese tecer; as well as English text, French tisser, Italian tessere, and Romanian țese.

parole.significato: to tend to, to have a tendency
parole.testo: Inherited from Old Spanish tender, from Latin tendō, -ere.

Inherited from Old Spanish tener (“to hold”), from Latin tenēre, teneō (“to hold; to keep; to have”), from Proto-Italic *tenēō, stative from Proto-Indo-European *ten- (“to stretch or draw”). The preterite forms in tuv- are from contamination with those of the nearly synonymous haber, hub-.
Learned borrowing from Latin tenuis. Cognate with English tenuous.

parole.significato: third, one of three equal parts
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin tertius. Doublet of tercia.
Inherited from Latin terrēnus.

parole.significato: Earth (planet of the Solar System in which all of humanity resides)
parole.testo: Inherited from Old Spanish tierra, from Latin terra, ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *ters- (“dry”).

Inherited from Latin tincta (“dyed”), perfect passive participle of tingō (“dye”, verb). Cognate with English tint, Dutch tint, Estonian tint, French teinte, German Tinte, Hungarian tinta, Italian tinta, Luxembourgish Tintin, and Portuguese tinta.
Borrowed from Latin toga.
Borrowed from Latin tollere. Doublet of tullir.
Inherited from Latin taurus (compare Italian toro, Portuguese touro, Romanian taur), from Proto-Indo-European *táwros. Doublet of Tauro.
Borrowed from Latin torqueō (“to twist”).
Inherited from Latin torreō. Cognate with English toast and torrent.
Inherited from Old Spanish tos, tose, from Latin tussis (“cough”).
Borrowed from Latin trāns (“across, on the far side, beyond”). Doublet of tras-, which was inherited.
Learned borrowing from Latin trānsversus. Doublet of travieso.

parole.significato: after, following, in the wake of; upon
parole.testo: Inherited from Old Spanish tras, from Latin trāns (“across, beyond”).
Inherited from Latin trānsversus.
Inherited from Latin trēs, from Proto-Italic *trēs, from Proto-Indo-European *tréyes.

Inherited from Latin tundēre (with change of conjugation), from Proto-Italic *tundō, nasal infix present from Proto-Indo-European *(s)tewd-, from *(s)tew- (“to push, hit”). Cognate with Old Irish do·tuit (“to fall”), Dutch stoten, German stoßen, English stot, Albanian shtyj (“to push”).
Borrowed from Latin tacitus.
Inherited from Latin tū, from Proto-Italic *tū, from Proto-Indo-European *túh₂. Cognate with English thou, Portuguese tu, Catalan tu, French tu, Italian tu, Romanian tu.
Inherited from Latin ūber, from Proto-Italic *ouðer, from Proto-Indo-European *h₁ówHdʰr̥ (“udder”).
